passage: Wastewater management is essential for maintaining public health and protecting our environment. When we use water in our homes, it becomes contaminated with various impurities. Many people mistakenly believe that only factory chemicals are pollutants, but organic waste like fruit and vegetable peels also degrade water quality. Similarly, pouring cooking oil down the sink is dangerous because it hardens in pipes, causing blockages, while flushing old medicines introduces harmful chemicals into the water supply. To treat this, wastewater first passes through bar screens, which physically remove large solid objects like plastic bags and sticks, not germs or chemicals. After screening, the water enters a tank where heavy solids settle at the bottom to form sludge. This sludge is not just useless trash; it is processed to produce biogas and manure. Finally, the water undergoes biological treatment where beneficial bacteria consume organic waste. While some bacteria are harmful, many are essential for cleaning water. It is a common myth that clear-looking river water is always safe; even transparent water can contain invisible pathogens that cause water-borne diseases. Therefore, we must treat wastewater carefully before it is released back into nature to ensure our water sources remain safe for everyone.

items.evidence: Similarly, pouring cooking oil down the sink is dangerous because it hardens in pipes, causing blockages, while flushing old medicines introduces harmful chemicals into the water supply.
items.q: Meena pours leftover cooking oil into the kitchen sink. What will most likely happen?
options: It turns solid in the pipes and clogs them
It flows away easily because it is liquid
It is caught later by the bar screens
It is harmless, like flushing old medicines
items.explain: Cooking oil hardens inside pipes and causes blockages, so it should never go down the sink.

wrong.why: thinks any liquid is safe to pour down the sink
thinks bar screens catch everything, not only large solids

items.evidence: To treat this, wastewater first passes through bar screens, which physically remove large solid objects like plastic bags and sticks, not germs or chemicals.
items.q: What does wastewater still contain right after it passes through the bar screens?
options: Germs and chemicals the screens cannot catch
Only harmless water, since screens kill germs
Plastic bags and sticks the screens let through
Sludge already turned into biogas and manure
items.explain: Bar screens only remove big objects like bags and sticks; germs and chemicals pass through.

wrong.why: thinks bar screens remove germs and chemicals
reverses what the screens actually remove
mixes up the order of treatment steps

items.evidence: This sludge is not just useless trash; it is processed to produce biogas and manure.
items.q: What happens to the heavy solids that settle at the bottom of the tank?
options: They are turned into fuel gas and fertiliser
They are thrown away as useless mud
They are eaten by bacteria in the tank
They are removed again by the bar screens
items.explain: The settled sludge is processed to make biogas and manure, so it is useful, not trash.

wrong.why: picks the nearby detail about bacteria eating waste
mixes up the screening and settling steps

items.q: Sunil's well water looks crystal clear. What should he understand before drinking it?
options: It may still carry germs too small to see
It is safe because it looks so clear
It is unsafe only if factories are near
It is unsafe because all bacteria are harmful
items.explain: Even transparent water can hold invisible germs that cause water-borne diseases.
